title: Rosi Braidotti
summary: Rosi Braidotti (b. 1954) is an Italian-Australian philosopher working in the Netherlands, an heir to Spinoza and Deleuze, and one of the leading theorists of posthumanism and feminism. She invites us to see the human being not as a separate master of nature but as a "nomadic subject" — a moving knot of connections with other people, animals, technologies and the planet.
onEmotions: Braidotti thinks about feelings through Spinoza and Deleuze: affects are what increase or decrease our capacity to act and to connect with the world (she calls this capacity potentia). She doesn't divide emotions into "good" and "bad" in a moral sense, but she distinguishes forces that drain us from forces that affirm life. Her "affirmative" ethics doesn't demand positive thinking and doesn't deny pain: it is about slowly, together with others, transforming passive suffering into an active force. For Braidotti, a person is a "nomadic subject", always in motion and in connection, so feelings never belong to them alone.

anxiety.text: Braidotti calls our time the "posthuman convergence": the fourth industrial revolution meeting the sixth mass extinction. No wonder anxiety is so recognisable today — it keenly registers the scale of these changes. Braidotti doesn't pretend this isn't frightening. But she offers a particular way of relating to such a state — "cartography": not trying to take in everything at once, but honestly mapping where you are, what is acting on you and what you are connected to. Anxiety feeds on vagueness; a map gives you back something concrete. Seen this way, your anxiety is sensitivity to the real world, not a malfunction. It can become a point of orientation: a way of noticing what in your situation truly depends on you, and who you are not alone with in it.
anxiety.practice: Take a sheet of paper and draw a map of your "here and now": you in the centre, arrows to what weighs on you and to what holds you. For Braidotti, cartography begins with an honest "I am here."

fear.text: A bridge is built for a certain load, and Braidotti, following Spinoza and Deleuze, says every body has similar "thresholds of sustainability" — limits to how much it can bear without breaking down. Your fear is a natural protection that deserves respect: often it signals that you have come close to such a threshold. Fear is not cowardice but knowledge about the limits of your strength. Braidotti also stresses that these thresholds aren't fixed once and for all: they widen when we are held by connections and narrow in isolation. So the point is not to heroically ignore fear, but to respect your limits and, gradually and in the company of others, expand what you are able to bear.
fear.practice: Stand up and slowly shift your weight from heels to toes and back until you find the point where you stand steadily. Remember that feeling: a threshold can be sensed with the body, not only with thought.

sadness.text: Spinoza, almost like a physicist, defines sadness as a passage to lesser power, a diminished capacity to act and feel. Braidotti takes this definition without the moralising — so there is no need to be ashamed of your sadness. Braidotti calls the capacity to act potentia — power as ability, as opposed to potestas, power as domination over others. By this logic, sadness is not a moral failure but an honest sense that, for a while, you have less strength. Braidotti's affirmative ethics doesn't ask you to pretend everything is fine. It asks a different question: which connections and encounters could gradually give you back your strength? In this light, sadness is not a dead end but a state you can pass through — especially if you don't stay in it alone.
sadness.practice: Arrange a small "Spinozist" encounter: go for ten minutes to a place where you usually feel a little lighter — a park, the river, a favourite bakery. Notice whether your strength has grown by even a drop.

grief.text: "Affirmative" in Braidotti does not mean "cheerful": her ethics of affirmation doesn't deny suffering and has nothing to do with positive thinking. Grief is an enormous pain, and no philosophy should explain it away. Her ethics is about the slow transformation of pain — about finding, over time and together with others, a way to go on living within it and to stay connected to the world. Braidotti is fond of the word "endurance", which holds both meanings: to bear and to last. Grief asks exactly this of us — not victory, but the ability to go on lasting alongside the pain. Your bond with what you have lost does not vanish: it keeps changing you and becomes part of who you are becoming. The love that was remains an active force.
grief.practice: Do something the way the one you lost used to do it: make tea their way, walk their route, say their favourite phrase. Let the bond last on through your body.

loneliness.text: Trillions of microbes live in your body: for Braidotti, a human being is never singular. Still, loneliness hurts — the pain of a being made for connection, not a sign of something broken. Braidotti describes the human being as a "nomadic subject" — not a closed-off unit but a moving knot of relations with other people, animals, places, technologies, the planet itself. Even when no one is around, these connections don't disappear entirely: you are held by the air you breathe, by food someone grew, by a language shaped over generations. At the same time, Braidotti doesn't erase differences: our experiences are not the same, and loneliness can come from your particularity going unseen. So loneliness is not a sign you are cut off from the world but a longing for connections where you will be accepted in your difference. Such connections are possible precisely because togetherness doesn't require sameness.
loneliness.practice: Go out for five minutes and greet — aloud or silently — three non-human neighbours: a tree, a dog, the wind. For Braidotti, the nomadic subject is always in company.

quote.text: We are in this together, but we are not one and the same.
quote.author: Rosi Braidotti

anger.text: Nietzsche divided forces into reactive ones, which only answer a blow, and active ones, which create — and Braidotti turns this distinction into an ethics. Your anger, especially in the face of injustice, is a legitimate feeling; the only question is which kind of force it will become. Reactive anger gets stuck in grievance: it returns to the wound again and again and keeps us tied to what hurt us. Braidotti doesn't condemn this kind of anger, but she shows that over time it drains us. The affirmative path is not to suppress anger but to transform its energy — to turn it into a force for creating, protecting, building different connections. Your anger is a valuable signal and a powerful charge. The question is not whether it is "right" to be angry, but where you want to direct this force so that it works for you rather than against you.
anger.practice: Channel the charge of anger into your body: five minutes of brisk walking, wall push-ups or vigorously cleaning one corner. Then ask yourself where this force wants to go next — to destroy or to build.

shame.text: Leonardo's Vitruvian Man, fitted into a perfect circle and square, quietly set a norm, Braidotti argues: male, European, healthy and able-bodied. Shame squeezes you precisely next to such a norm: it feels as though you don't measure up to what a person should be — though this "proper human" is itself a historical construction. Everything that differed from it was treated as deviation. Braidotti proposes a posthuman view in which difference is not a flaw but a feature of life. For her the subject is "nomadic" — always in process, never frozen. Seen this way, shame tries to fix you in a single image: "I am bad." But you are not a finished portrait; you are movement. The way you don't fit the norm may simply be your way of being alive.
shame.practice: Stand and spread your arms like the Vitruvian Man — then step out of the perfect circle: bend, slouch, take any posture of your own. Say aloud: "This is human too."

guilt.text: A spider that touches one thread feels the whole web tremble — this is roughly how Braidotti sees responsibility: we are knots in a web, and our actions echo far. Guilt can be honest when you really have hurt someone. Rosi Braidotti, following Nietzsche and Deleuze, is wary of a culture of guilt that keeps people in constant self-accusation and paralyses them. Instead, she speaks of accountability — the ability to recognise your place in a web of connections and how your actions affect it. The difference is subtle but important: guilt looks backwards and asks "how bad am I?", while accountability looks forward and asks "what can be done now?". Your guilt can become a starting point not for punishing yourself, but for action that repairs connections and makes the world a little better.
guilt.practice: Take one repairing step today: a short message, returning something, an offer to help. Not "how guilty am I?" but "what can I mend in the web right now?"

envy.text: Two Latin powers, potestas and potentia — Braidotti doesn't write about envy directly, but this distinction seems made for that prickly and very human feeling. Potestas is power as domination: status, position, a place in the hierarchy. There is never enough of it to go round, and people have to compete for it. Potentia is power as capacity: the ability to act, feel, create, connect with others. It grows when it is shared. Braidotti would probably note that envy is almost always looking at potestas: the other person seems to have more room, recognition, success. But what makes life truly rich lies in the realm of potentia, and someone else's success doesn't take it away from you. You might ask yourself: what capacity — rather than status — do I actually want to develop?
envy.practice: Imagine all the status you envy were taken away, leaving only the skill. Which skill from that other life would you want to take? Name it — that is your potentia, and you can start learning it.

emptiness.text: The ancient Greeks distinguished bios — the life of an individual with a biography — from zoe, life as such; Braidotti puts zoe at the centre. Emptiness can be heavy: it feels as though nothing inside is moving. Rosi Braidotti invites us to look at life more broadly than our personal experiences. She speaks of zoe — the vital force that runs through everything alive, not only through humans: through plants, animals, the cells of our bodies. Zoe doesn't ask whether we're in the mood right now — it simply keeps working: the heart beats, the breath goes on, the body repairs itself. Your "self" may feel empty, but life in you doesn't stop. This isn't a demand to "cheer up" but a quiet support: you don't have to produce all the meaning on your own. Sometimes it's enough just to be near something that lives — a plant, an animal, the sky.
emptiness.practice: For two minutes do nothing — just put your fingers on your wrist and feel your pulse. That is zoe working without your effort; you don't need to produce any meaning right now.

confusion.text: A compass is useless until you know where you're standing — and that is where Braidotti begins. Confusion is frightening, but for Rosi Braidotti it is almost the natural state of the contemporary person. Her "nomadic subject" lives in motion, without an identity fixed once and for all. Drawing on Deleuze and Foucault, Braidotti offers an important distinction: the actual — what we are ceasing to be — and the virtual — what we are becoming. Confusion often arises exactly at this seam: the old self is already leaving, and the new one hasn't taken shape yet. Braidotti advises not rushing into a new rigid identity, but drawing up a "cartography" of the moment — describing where you are now and which forces are acting on you. Seen this way, confusion is not losing yourself but a sign that you are in the process of becoming.
confusion.practice: Write two lines: "Who I am ceasing to be: …" and "Who I may be becoming: …" You can leave the second unfinished — becoming doesn't like full stops.

fatigue.text: Braidotti has an unexpectedly gentle word for philosophy — "sustainability," as with an ecosystem that cannot be exploited endlessly. Tiredness and burnout signal that you have been working at your limit for a long time. Rosi Braidotti writes about sustainability not as endless endurance but as the ability not to break down: every body has its thresholds, and respecting them is an ethical choice, not a defeat. She criticises contemporary "cognitive capitalism", which expects constant productivity, flexibility and self-improvement from people. Braidotti's affirmative ethics isn't about heroism or pushing through at any cost. It's about preserving the strength to live and create by sharing the load and leaning on others. Rest is not laziness but a way of staying in living connection with the world for the long haul.
fatigue.practice: Lie on the floor for five minutes with your arms spread and do nothing — like a field left fallow. The earth, too, needs seasons when nothing grows on it.

boredom.text: The nomad, for Braidotti, needn't travel: the greatest journeys, she writes, can happen without moving. Boredom can be oppressive — she doesn't write about it directly, but her philosophy of becoming explains a lot. For Braidotti, life is a continuous process of change and encounter, and a person is a knot of connections with a vast world, not only a human one. Boredom may arise when this flow narrows to a tight circle of familiar stimuli — a screen, a routine, the same old thoughts. The posthuman view invites you to widen your attention beyond the human: to notice birds, weather, plants, your own body, the technologies through which you live. The world is full of processes happening right now. In this light, boredom is not an absence of anything interesting but an invitation to reconnect with what is already living and changing around you.
boredom.practice: Take a "journey without moving": for five minutes look out of the window and count how many different non-human lives are moving there — birds, clouds, leaves, insects.

joy.text: A sprout breaks through asphalt not because the asphalt softened but because the sprout has force — Braidotti thinks of joy in much this way. Your joy is no trifle but one of the most important forces of life. Following Spinoza, she understands joy as the experience of our capacity to act, feel and connect with the world increasing. Braidotti's affirmative ethics is built around such moments: they are not a naive escape from problems but a source of strength that helps us live and stand up to what is hard. Braidotti stresses that joy doesn't cancel pain or require us to forget it. It simply shows the direction in which life can grow. Your joy is a valuable compass: it points to the encounters, activities and connections that make you stronger. You can not only live it but also remember it as a clue.
joy.practice: Share this joy with someone right now — call, send a photo, tell them over dinner. For Braidotti, potentia grows when it is shared.

love.text: Spinoza has a simple yardstick for love: do you become stronger and more alive beside the other? Braidotti, following him and Deleuze, sees love above all as a mutual increase of power, and tenderness as an encounter that changes both. Her nomadic view rejects love as possession: the other is not property and not the "other half" you were missing, but a living being on their own path, with whom you have fallen into step. Braidotti also extends love beyond the human: tenderness towards an animal, a place, the planet is no less real for her. Your love is not a weakness or a dependency but one of the most powerful ways of becoming yourself together with others.
love.practice: Ask this person today — or yourself about them: "What have you become able to do since being with me?" Spinoza's yardstick works both ways.

gratitude.text: A third of what we eat exists thanks to bees and other pollinators — and Braidotti suggests seeing gratitude not as politeness but as knowledge of how life works. Gratitude is a feeling in which it becomes clear that we don't live alone. Rosi Braidotti invites us to extend this thought to the scale of all life: we are not separate masters of the world but part of a vast web in which people, animals, plants, microorganisms, machines and the elements support one another. Braidotti calls this view "zoe-centred" — attention to life in all its forms, not only to the human. Gratitude is the ability to notice countless supports: the tree that gives shade, the bees pollinating plants, people whose labour remains invisible. Such gratitude doesn't make us small; it makes us connected. And it reminds us that we, too, can be a support for others.
gratitude.practice: Do one small thing in return for the non-human world: water a plant, scatter crumbs for the birds, switch off an unneeded light. Gratitude, for Braidotti, is an exchange, not just words.

hope.text: A seed in the soil shows nothing yet but is already at work — Braidotti loves such images of the future. For her, hope is not a naive expectation that everything will sort itself out, but an active force. Her affirmative ethics faces the future: it invites us to think about what the world could become and to invest in that becoming right now. Braidotti draws on Deleuze's notion of the "virtual" — not the unreal, but the not-yet-actualised, what is ripening in the present as a possibility. Hope is sensitivity to the virtual, to what may grow out of present connections. Braidotti stresses that such a future is built together, not alone. So your hope doesn't have to be certainty about the outcome. It can simply be a readiness to take part in what is only just being born.
hope.practice: Plant something — a seed in a pot, a cutting in a glass of water — or simply put a branch in water. Let a small "virtual" future stand on the windowsill.

nostalgia.text: Braidotti argues against social nostalgia — longing for the "good old days" and for the human as master of the world: such longing, she thinks, keeps us from seeing the present. But your personal, tender longing for the past is another matter, and there is nothing shameful in it. In personal memory Braidotti finds another possibility too. Following Deleuze, Braidotti understands memory not as an archive you can return to but as a creative force: in remembering, we reassemble the past anew and discover in it the seeds of the future. Nostalgia is not only a backward glance. What you loved then can become a resource for who you are becoming now.
nostalgia.practice: Take out an old photo or object from the past and look at it as if for the first time. Find one detail you never noticed before — for Braidotti, memory is not an archive but a workshop.

craving.text: Deleuze, after Spinoza, asked: "What can a body do?" Braidotti adds: "How much can it bear?" — and asks this of every urge instead of "is it good or bad?". A sharp "I want it right now" can sweep through your whole body like a wave, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. She speaks of "thresholds of sustainability": everyone has a limit beyond which what seems to add life begins to take it away. Braidotti is wary of romanticising "going beyond the limits" and insists that only experience that can be sustained and prolonged without destroying yourself is valuable. A craving is not a vice but a force seeking an outlet — one that, in this form, drains you. You don't have to suppress it or act on it at once; you can watch it: the wave rises, peaks and subsides. And you remain.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, rate its strength from 1 to 10 and set a timer for five minutes. Then rate it again: the wave moves, and you are the observer on the shore.

addiction.text: A dammed river doesn't disappear — it just runs through one narrow channel; Braidotti describes the force of life, potentia, in much the same way. When life has long been organised around one thing, it isn't a moral failure but a circle that is hard to break. Braidotti distinguishes two senses of power: potestas — power that restricts and captures — and potentia — the capacity to act, connect, grow. Addiction can be described as a situation in which one connection gradually crowds out all the others and narrows potentia to a single tight channel. Braidotti offers neither condemnation nor a heroic leap. Her affirmative ethics is a slow, shared transformation of a draining force into a sustaining one: adding connections, not just taking away the habit. For her the subject is nomadic, always in motion — so no circle is your final essence.
addiction.practice: Name one connection that gives you strength at no cost — a person, a place, an activity — and give it five minutes today. If you'd like, a mutual-help group can become such a connection too: a channel widens through its tributaries.

hangover.text: Descartes thought the mind could be separated from the body — Braidotti disagrees, and the morning after is the most vivid argument on her side. Your body aches, and thoughts about yesterday bring anxiety and shame. Braidotti insists that we are "embodied and embedded" subjects: not a mind that happens to be placed in a body, but the body itself, bound up with its surroundings. That's why the physical and the moral hangover are intertwined: the body is depleted, and thoughts take on the darkest colours. The first step is not to judge yesterday but to care for the body: rest, fresh air, quiet. Braidotti speaks of "thresholds of sustainability" — how much a body can bear. A hangover can be understood as a message about such a threshold, not as proof that something is wrong with you. Sorting out yesterday is better left for later, when your strength returns.
hangover.practice: Open a window and take ten breaths of fresh air, then wash your face with cool water. Tell yourself: "Body first, thoughts later."

euphoria.text: In spring the buds open almost at once, as if on a signal — Braidotti calls this impersonal force shared by all living things zoe: life in its excessive, creative surge. A burst of elation, when everything seems possible, is that force in a very vivid form, and there's no need to be suspicious of it right away. In euphoria we seem to feel this flow directly. Following Spinoza, Braidotti values joy as an affect that increases potentia — the capacity to act and connect with the world. But she also reminds us of thresholds of sustainability: a force is good when it can be sustained and prolonged. You can live and enjoy euphoria while also noticing which connections and ideas it has lit up — they may outlast the burst itself.
euphoria.practice: Write down one connection or idea this joy has made brighter, and set a reminder to come back to the note in a week.

crash.text: High tide and low tide are the same ocean, and Braidotti sees life in a similar way. A sharp drop after a high can be agonising — as if all your energy had been pumped out of you. Braidotti describes life as a flow of forces that swells and ebbs, and the body has its own "thresholds of sustainability". After an intense high — a celebration, a success, a turbulent event — comes a comedown, because energy isn't infinite. The crash is not a punishment and not a sign that the joy was fake, but the rhythm of a living body that needs to recover. Braidotti's affirmative ethics doesn't ask you to stay at the peak: it teaches you to build up strength slowly, leaning on your connections with other people and with the world. You can give yourself time: the comedown is also part of the movement, not its end.
crash.practice: Take a slow ten-minute walk — half your usual speed, no goal, no headphones. Low tide is part of the rhythm too: let your body choose the pace.

panic.text: Roots hold a tree in a storm not because the wind weakens but because the tree has grown into the earth — an image close to Braidotti's thinking. A wave of panic is frightening: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it feels as though disaster is about to strike. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Braidotti, following Spinoza, thinks of a person as a body through which intense forces pass — and sometimes their flow becomes too strong. For her, we are not separate fortresses but beings "embedded" in the world: we are held by the ground, the air, objects, other living things. In a moment of panic you can lean on exactly these connections — not on a mind racing to explain everything, but on what physically surrounds you. The wave passes through the body, but the body stays connected to the world that holds it.
panic.practice: Sit down and press your palms firmly into the seat or the floor, like roots into the earth. Breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and name aloud five things you can see around you.

dread.text: The atoms of your body were once stardust, trees, other bodies — Braidotti invites us to think of life on that scale. When the question "what is all this for?" and the thought of finitude sweep over you, the dread can be enormous, and Braidotti doesn't brush it aside. She speaks of zoe — the impersonal force of life that flows through all living things and belongs to no one in particular. We are not owners of life but participants in it, connected to countless other beings — those who came before us and those who will come after. Meaning isn't hidden somewhere outside the world, and it doesn't have to be proven: it takes shape in connections, in how you affect others and others affect you. Braidotti's affirmative ethics is not a once-and-for-all answer to the abyss, but daily care for what is alive now, together with others.
dread.practice: In the evening, go outside or to a window and find the sky. For a minute, stay with the thought that you are a participant in a life older and wider than you, not its sole owner.

fomo.text: A shop window is lit brighter than the street — that's its purpose — and Braidotti sees our era turning whole lives into such windows. The feeling that everyone else lives more vividly while you're in the wrong place is a very recognisable pain of our time. Braidotti describes contemporary capitalism as a system that speeds everything up and turns desires and attention into commodities. The social media feed is part of that machine: it sells an image of a life in which something is always happening, and it keeps fuelling a sense of lack. The fear of missing out isn't your personal flaw but an effect of a system that profits from restlessness. Braidotti proposes "cartography" — a careful description of where you actually are: which people, places and activities you are connected to. Such a map is usually richer than it seems when you're looking at other people's shop windows.
fomo.practice: Put your phone down and make a spoken "map of here": say aloud three people, two places and one activity you are connected to right now.

sleepless.text: Night, for Braidotti, is not empty: owls, moths and night-blooming flowers live in their own rhythm, and you are part of that same world. When you can't sleep, thoughts run in circles, and it wears you out. Braidotti reminds us that we are bodily beings embedded in the rhythms of the world: day and night, light and darkness, work and rest. Modern life increasingly blurs these rhythms — screens, work without boundaries, constant availability. Then insomnia is tied not only to personal worries but also to a world that doesn't let the body stop in time. You don't have to turn it into yet another task that must be solved urgently. Braidotti emphasises our connection with the non-human world — with air, silence, breath. At three in the morning these connections haven't gone anywhere. You can simply be with them, without demanding sleep of yourself.
sleepless.practice: Listen to the night and silently name everything, living or not, that is sounding now: the wind, the house, someone's breathing, a distant car. Don't chase sleep — just make a sound map of the night.

betrayal.text: Braidotti thinks of the human being as a nomadic subject woven from connections — and fabric tears where it was stretched tightest. Betrayal wounds precisely where you were open, and that pain deserves acknowledgement: we don't exist apart from those we love and trust. That's why betrayal feels like a tear in the very fabric you are made of. Braidotti doesn't demand that you quickly forgive or "let go". Her affirmative ethics is slow work: pain and anger are acknowledged, and then gradually, together with others, transformed from a destructive force into one that lets you go on living. Betrayal doesn't cancel your capacity for connection; it shows which connection turned out to be fragile. The web that holds you is wider than one person — and you can see it anew.
betrayal.practice: Call or message someone who stayed close despite this wound and simply say: "Thank you for being here." The web is wider than one torn thread.

jealousy.text: A butterfly can only be held by closing your fist — and Braidotti distinguishes two powers: potestas, which wants to possess and fix in place, and potentia, a force that grows through connection. Jealousy seizes both body and mind: you want to hold on, to control, not to lose. Jealousy can be understood as a moment when love, which was potentia, starts reaching towards potestas: to hold on to the other, to fix them in one form. Braidotti doesn't shame you for this: fear of loss is the natural reaction of a being who treasures a connection. But her nomadic thinking reminds us that both you and the other are always in motion. Love that doesn't try to stop that motion becomes stronger. You might ask yourself: what would help me feel safe without holding on to the other by force?
jealousy.practice: Clench your fist, hold it for ten seconds — then slowly open your palm. Notice which feels calmer, holding or releasing — and ask: what can I do for my own safety myself?

resentment.text: Nietzsche compared grievance to indigestion: a person cannot "have done" with what happened, and it keeps coming back up. Long-held resentment really is heavy — you carry it for years, and it wears down your strength. Braidotti, following Spinoza and Nietzsche, distinguishes affects that increase our capacity to act from those that decrease it. Nietzsche called long-festering grievance ressentiment — a pain that returns you to the past again and again, binding you to the moment when harm was done. Braidotti doesn't ask you to pretend the harm didn't happen. Her affirmative ethics isn't forgetting but slow transformation: turning passive pain into an active force that opens up the future. Your resentment holds a truth, but it doesn't have to define your whole life. Such transformation doesn't happen on command — it's a process in which the support of others matters a great deal.
resentment.practice: Imagine that the strength going into this resentment came back to you for one evening. Where would you spend it? Take the smallest step in that direction today.

heartbreak.text: One of Braidotti's books is called Metamorphoses — and a caterpillar in its cocoon literally dissolves before it becomes something new. A broken heart hurts on every level — in the body and in your thoughts about the future. Braidotti says we are nomadic subjects: our self is made up of connections, and when one of the most important ones breaks, we lose a part of ourselves. That's why a breakup is so disorienting. But being nomadic also means something else: you were never a frozen portrait; you are always in the process of becoming. In Metamorphoses Braidotti describes change not as a comforting formula but as the very fabric of life: experience, including painful experience, changes us. A breakup is not the end of your story but a painful turn in a movement that continues. The love you lived remains part of the strength you carry forward.
heartbreak.practice: Walk somewhere you never went together — a new street, a different park. Notice that this space isn't taken up by anything yet: the next chapter can begin here.

impostor.text: Classical humanism painted a portrait of the "real" person — confident, self-sufficient, rational, without a shadow of doubt — and Braidotti sees in it the yardstick by which we still picture the competent professional. The feeling that you're here by accident and about to be found out is exhausting. But this ideal, for Braidotti, is a historical construction, not a description of real people. The nomadic subject is never final — it is always learning, changing, on the way. Your sense that "I'm not quite in my place yet" is not an exposure but an honest feeling of movement. No one arrives at a point of final competence. Your doubts are a sign that you are growing, not frozen in a role.
impostor.practice: Compare yourself not with an imaginary "real expert" but with yourself a year ago. Write down one thing you've learned since then — that is the nomadic path.

self_hatred.text: Spinoza advised judging every thought by whether it adds strength or takes it away, and Braidotti applies this even to the loudest inner voice. Your inner critic can sound so sure that it seems like the truth. For Braidotti, who follows Spinoza here, self-hatred is an affect that diminishes our potentia, our capacity to act and connect with the world. Such affects bring no self-knowledge — they only drain us. Braidotti stresses that affirmative ethics is neither positive thinking nor an order to love yourself immediately. It is a slow transformation: step by step, ceasing to believe the forces that devalue life and leaning on the forces that sustain it. Seen this way, the critic isn't telling the truth about you; it speaks the language of norms that demand you be someone else. You are more than that voice: you are a multitude of connections, holding both worth and care.
self_hatred.practice: Say the critic's phrase out loud, then answer it with a fact from your life: "Yesterday I helped…", "My cat is waiting for me…" Spinoza would call this setting one affect against another.

helplessness.text: One ant can't move a twig, but an anthill builds a whole city — Braidotti likes such reminders of non-human wisdom. Feeling powerless to change anything is one of the heaviest feelings, and it often reflects real constraints. Braidotti distinguishes potestas — power that restricts and suppresses — from potentia — the capacity to act that every living being has. When potestas presses down, it seems that no potentia is left at all. But Braidotti insists that potentia is by its nature bound up with others: it grows in relationships. Where one person can't manage, many together can. Helplessness speaks of the limits of your solitary effort, not the limits of life. Affirmative ethics begins small: find one connection that adds strength, and lean on it.
helplessness.practice: Call or message one person who is also thinking about this problem and say: "I've been thinking about it too." Every anthill starts like that.

procrastination.text: In "cognitive capitalism," as Braidotti calls our economy, the main resources are knowledge, attention and creative energy, and the system demands constant productivity and readiness. Against that background, "I can't get started" easily turns into self-blame. The system's pressure feels like personal responsibility, although it is largely systemic. Procrastination is sometimes a signal about a threshold of sustainability: body and mind are saying "too much". Braidotti suggests asking not "why am I being lazy?" but "what right now increases my capacity to act, and what drains it?". Getting started is often easier not through forcing yourself, but through connection — with curiosity, with another person, with a small part of the task that resonates with you.
procrastination.practice: Find the part of the task you're most curious about — not the first in order, but the living one — and work on it for five minutes. Becoming rarely follows a list.

uprooted.text: Italy, Australia, France, the Netherlands — Braidotti has lived several lives in different languages and made the figure of the nomad central to her philosophy. Emigration or moving can feel like losing the ground beneath your feet, and this pain is real. The nomadic subject is not a homeless person, and not necessarily even a traveller, but someone who learns to live in motion without losing connections. For her, nomadism is not an absence of roots but a different relationship to them: roots become mobile and interwoven, like a web. Braidotti also writes about life between languages as a distinctive, rich experience. Your uprootedness is not only a loss but also the beginning of a new map on which old and new connections intertwine. Your former home doesn't disappear: it becomes part of who you are becoming along the way.
uprooted.practice: Say aloud one word in the language of your former home and one word you like in the language of the new place. Life between languages, for Braidotti, is not a gap but a wealth.

quote.text: The nomadic subject is a myth, that is to say a political fiction, that allows me to think through and move across established categories and levels of experience.
quote.author: Rosi Braidotti

overload.text: A phone weighs a couple of hundred grams, yet more information passes through it in a day than a person of earlier centuries met in years — Braidotti calls our era "posthuman": we have grown into networks, and the line between us and machines keeps thinning. The endless feed, notifications and news can overload you to the limit. Braidotti doesn't call for giving up technology, but she asks a Spinozist question: how much can a body bear? Today many people run up against their "thresholds of sustainability" because the flow of information grows faster than our capacity to take it in. Overload isn't your inability to "cope" but a signal that a threshold has been reached. Braidotti reminds us that we are "embodied and embedded" beings. Returning to the body and the space around you is not escapism but a way of restoring your strength.
overload.practice: Put the screen in another room and listen to the sounds around you for three minutes. Notice where in your body things have become a little quieter — that's the threshold moving back.

unreality.text: For Braidotti, thought always comes from somewhere: a particular body, place and time — there is no "view from nowhere." She doesn't write directly about the feeling that the world, or you yourself, isn't real, but her thinking helps speak of it gently: reality is felt through the body and through connections. She insists that we are "embodied and embedded" subjects: not an abstract mind hovering above the world, but bodies rooted in a specific place, time and environment. When life becomes too tense or too screen-bound, this rootedness can weaken. The return of reality begins with simple things: feeling your feet on the floor, touching an object, hearing a sound outside the window. These connections haven't gone anywhere — they have just grown quieter.
unreality.practice: Stand up, feel your body's weight on your feet and say aloud where you are, what time of day it is and what the weather is outside. That is your point on the map.

awe.text: The starlight you see set out before you were born — Braidotti loves such reminders of scale. Awe before something vast or beautiful is one of the deepest experiences. For Braidotti, in such awe you can sense zoe — the impersonal force of life that flows through everything alive, from a human to a tree to a microbe. Her posthumanism invites you to see yourself not as the crown of creation but as part of an enormous web of life. In awe this thought becomes tangible: you are a small part and, at the same time, connected to something greater. This doesn't diminish you; it frees you from the need to be the centre of the world. Braidotti values affects that widen our connection with the world, and awe is one of the most powerful. You can simply let it in and let it change how you see.
awe.practice: Be silent for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, and silently list the living beings sharing this place with you now — from people to grass to invisible microbes.

relief.text: A released spring returns to its shape — Braidotti, following Spinoza, sees relief as the same kind of return of potentia, our capacity to act and connect with the world. What was pressing on you finally lets go, and the body relaxes. While we were under pressure, this force was compressed; now it can flow again. Relief is not merely the absence of something bad but an affirmative affect worth noticing and feeling fully. Braidotti's affirmative ethics isn't about constantly waiting for new troubles but about paying attention to what increases life. Relief is exactly such a moment. You can give yourself time to feel your strength returning, and not rush to load it with new tasks straight away.
relief.practice: Stretch your whole body as after a long sleep, and notice where strength is returning — shoulders, back, arms. Give yourself a few more minutes without new tasks.

calm.text: A tree grows more slowly than we scroll a feed — and Braidotti sees such slow rhythms as an antidote to an accelerating world. Calm and peace are rare in a world that keeps speeding up. Braidotti describes advanced capitalism as a system in which everything moves faster and demands constant reaction from us. Against this background, calm is almost a form of resistance, a way of keeping your own rhythm. Braidotti would probably say that calm is not passivity but a time when strength accumulates and is restored, when the body lives in harmony with its thresholds of sustainability. In calm it's easier to feel your connection with the slow rhythms of the world — breathing, the passing of the day, the growth of plants. Nomadic thought doesn't set movement against rest: even a nomad stops for the night. Allow yourself this stop — it is part of the journey.
calm.practice: Find something nearby that lives slowly — a plant, the clouds, light on the wall — and watch it for three minutes, breathing at its pace.

inspiration.text: Barbara McClintock discovered "jumping genes" that move around the chromosome, and Braidotti borrowed the image for her book Transpositions: life keeps reshuffling its material. Inspiration feels like such a jump — a current flowing through you and the urge to create. For Braidotti, creativity never belongs to a single self: we are nomadic subjects through whom forces, ideas and influences pass — from other people, books, places and even non-human beings. Inspiration is a moment when these currents are especially tangible and you become their conduit. Braidotti, following Deleuze, speaks of "becoming" — a process in which we are constantly turning into something new. Inspiration is becoming, experienced from within. You can cherish it without clinging to it or demanding an immediate result. Even if the current ebbs, its trace will remain in you as a grown capacity to see and create.
inspiration.practice: Hum any familiar tune, then the same one a little higher or lower. That is transposition: the same, but otherwise. Try "transposing" your idea the same way — one sentence, out loud.

schadenfreude.text: Braidotti, following Spinoza, distinguishes two forces: potentia — our own capacity to live and act, rather like a root — and potestas, power as a ladder, where hierarchy and comparison decide everything. Schadenfreude is an unpleasant discovery about yourself, but a very human one. Schadenfreude usually flares up where we are living inside the logic of potestas: someone is higher, someone lower, and another person's fall seems to lift us up a step. This feeling speaks not of your "corrupt nature" but of how deeply competition is built into us. Joy at someone else's failure doesn't add to your strength — it only shifts your place on the ladder for a moment. Noticing this is already a step towards a different joy, one that grows out of your own strength rather than someone else's weakness.
schadenfreude.practice: Picture a ladder and, in your mind, step off it onto the ground. Ask yourself: what am I lacking right now — not compared with anyone, but simply for living?

contempt.text: A border on a map looks natural until you learn who drew it — Braidotti looks at many divisions between people this way. Contempt gives a sense of clarity and superiority, and sometimes shields us from what hurts too much. Braidotti shows how classical humanism built the image of the "real human" through disdain for "others": women, strangers, animals, everything bodily. For her, contempt is one of the ways of drawing an "us and them" line and freezing on one side of it. Her idea of the nomadic subject offers something else: you are not a fortress but a moving knot of connections, and what you despise is often tied to you more closely than you'd like. Contempt doesn't need to be uprooted by force. You can explore it like a map: where does the boundary I'm guarding run? What does it protect in me — and hasn't it become too narrow?
contempt.practice: Imagine an ordinary day of the one you despise: the morning, the commute, the tiredness in the evening. Find one point in that day where your lives are alike.

disgust.text: For Braidotti, mould, worms and decay are the work of the same life that flows through us. Disgust is an ancient, bodily feeling: it makes us recoil before we have time to think. Braidotti insists that we are "embodied and embedded" beings: thought is not separate from the body, nor the body from its environment. So for her, disgust is not a whim but a reaction of the whole organism, one worth respecting. But she also shows that culture often teaches disgust: towards bodiliness, old age, the "unclean", other kinds of living beings. Part of your disgust really does protect you, while part of it is a learned boundary. And if it is turned on yourself, remember: your body is not a mistake but a stretch of the same life that Braidotti calls by the Greek word zoe — the impersonal, stubborn force of the living, shared by all.
disgust.practice: When disgust rolls in, notice where it resonates in your body and take three slow breaths out through your mouth. Ask: is this protecting me right now — or is it an old rule I was taught?

revenge.text: A boomerang comes back to the one who threw it — Braidotti, following Nietzsche and Deleuze, calls the force of revenge "reactive": it is entirely defined by whoever hurt us and ties us to them again and again. The desire for revenge is a natural response to pain that has been inflicted, and there is nothing shameful in the desire itself. Revenge promises to restore the balance, but in fact it makes the offender the centre of our life. Braidotti's affirmative ethics suggests neither suppressing this energy nor being ashamed of it, but slowly recasting negative affects into a force that works for life. The wish for revenge shows how important the thing that was hurt really was. The same force can become self-protection, recovery, new boundaries — and you will stop revolving around the person who caused the pain.
revenge.practice: Write down what exactly was hurt — dignity, trust, safety. Next to it, one action that would restore it without involving the offender at all.

anger_at_loved.text: Boats tied side by side knock against each other on every wave: the tighter the bond, the more friction. Anger at the people close to us comes precisely because they are close. For Braidotti, the subject is not a closed-off self but a web of relations; we are literally woven from those we live with. That's why in closeness it isn't only feelings that collide, but also rhythms, needs and limits of endurance. Braidotti speaks of "thresholds of sustainability" — the limits up to which we can bear tension without breaking down. Anger at a partner, parent or child often means that such a threshold has been reached, not that you love badly. There's no need to be ashamed of the feeling itself. What matters is noticing what you're short of — rest, help, space of your own — and taking care of it, without unleashing that force on the people around you.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger rises, step outside or into another room for five minutes and ask yourself: which of my thresholds has been crossed — sleep, quiet, help? Come back with one request instead of a reproach.

ambivalence.text: A traveller who loves mountains and fears heights is still an ordinary traveller: Braidotti's nomadic self holds contradictory forces the same way. Loving someone and not bearing them at once is not a contradiction to resolve urgently but the ordinary fabric of closeness. Braidotti thinks along with Deleuze: the subject is not a solid monolith but a multiplicity in which different forces act at once. The nomadic self needn't hold one final attitude towards a person; it passes through different states. Your mixed feelings are an honest reflection of the fact that the relationship is alive and complex: it holds both what strengthens you and what drains you. You don't need to decide which feeling is the "real" one. You can map them instead — Braidotti is fond of the word "cartography": noting what exactly in this connection gives you strength and what takes it away.
ambivalence.practice: Draw two paths from yourself to this person: on one, mark what gives you strength; on the other, what takes it away. No conclusions — it's just a map of the terrain.

guilty_relief.text: A diver who surfaces gulps the air, and no one accuses them of not loving the sea. Relief you're ashamed of is one of the quietest, loneliest feelings: after a breakup, leaving a job, or long care for a seriously ill loved one. Braidotti, drawing on Spinoza, sees us as beings of limited endurance: each of us can bear strain only up to a certain threshold, and prolonged strain drains potentia — the power to live and act. When it ends, body and soul straighten up. That is what relief is, and it doesn't cancel your love. Love and relief, Braidotti would probably say, belong to different layers of one life and can sit side by side. Relief is not betrayal but a sign of how hard it was for you. You can let it be, the way you exhale after holding your breath.
guilty_relief.practice: Take a deep breath, hold it for a count of five and breathe out slowly. Tell yourself: "I loved — and it was very hard for me. Both truths are real."

indifference.text: Skin that is rubbed for a long time loses sensitivity — and Braidotti thinks something similar can happen to feelings. When something ought to move you and inside it's quiet, it's frightening, but it doesn't make you heartless. Braidotti describes our time as a stream of alarming news, crises and demands that no one can answer wholeheartedly forever. She speaks of "sustainability" not as heroic endurance but as the search for a rhythm of life that can actually be sustained. Indifference can be understood as a protective lowering of sensitivity once a threshold has already been crossed, rather than as callousness. What's more, for Braidotti, affects don't belong to us alone — they are born in connections. When connections are depleted, the response grows quiet. You can give it time to return through what is small, near and bodily, rather than by demanding that you immediately feel "the way you should".
indifference.practice: Find one small thing that stirs even a faint response — the smell of coffee, warm water on your hands, a sound outside — and stay with it for a minute, as with a first shoot.

escape.text: The nomad is the main character of Braidotti's philosophy, and she would not call the urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — a whim. But her "nomadism" isn't necessarily a physical move: it is the ability not to freeze in a single identity, to keep moving, to cross boundaries within yourself. The wish to escape may be a signal that a role has become too tight, that you have outgrown some form of life. It isn't irresponsibility but the voice of your capacity for movement. You don't have to decide anything big right away. You can start with a small nomadic step — change a route, a habit, the people you spend time with — and sense where you are really being drawn: away from something, or towards something new.
escape.practice: Take a small nomadic step today: walk home by an unfamiliar route or look into a place you've never been. Notice where you are drawn — away from something, or towards something.

forbidden_attraction.text: For Braidotti and Deleuze, desire is not a hole to be filled but an engine: a creative force, a striving for connection and for the expansion of life. Attraction to someone who is "off limits" can be confusing and unsettling. In her view, desire is always bigger than a single person: through someone specific we are drawn towards a particular quality, possibility, way of being. Such an attraction tells you something about yourself — about what kind of life, or what part of yourself, you are missing right now. It demands neither immediate action nor a verdict. You can look at it as a map of your forces: what exactly draws you so strongly to this person? And what place could that quality take in your own life?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Silently name one quality that draws you to this person — courage, lightness, freedom. Imagine what that quality might look like in your own life a month from now.

social_anxiety.text: Confident, talkative, always saying the right thing — Braidotti sees in this image an invisible norm of our time, one people punish themselves for failing. Shyness and the fear of being judged turn an ordinary conversation into an ordeal. This image, like the classical ideal of the Vitruvian Man, is not universal at all: it passes off one way of being as the yardstick for everyone. Braidotti's nomadic subject doesn't have to match the norm; difference is not a defect but a way of living. Besides, in her view, we are connected to others not only by words but also by presence, attention and bodily closeness. You don't need to be a brilliant conversationalist to truly take part. Quiet attention is also a connection. Perhaps someone near you is feeling exactly the same.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, choose one person and simply listen closely — with a nod, a look, one question. For Braidotti, presence is a full connection too.

uncertainty.text: Desert nomads navigate by stars and wind, not a ready-made map — Braidotti sees in them a model for our time. Uncertainty is tiring: you want something to rely on. Braidotti describes our time as an era of deep transitions — technological, ecological, social — when many familiar landmarks are shaken. She doesn't promise certainty. But her nomadic subject lives in motion from the start: it doesn't look for a final point of support but learns to find its way as it goes. Braidotti calls this a "cartography of the present" — the ability to map what is happening now without the illusion that the whole road is known in advance. Uncertainty is not a sign that you're lost but the ordinary condition of being on the way. You can lean not on knowledge of the future but on connections: the people, habits and places that hold you here and now.
uncertainty.practice: Take a short walk with no route: at each corner, choose your direction by whatever calls you — light, a tree, a sound. Notice that finding your way as you go is a skill too.

waiting.text: A seed under snow isn't just waiting for spring — it is living its winter life, and Braidotti invites us to see pauses that way. Waiting drags on: it's as if life has been put on pause until the answer comes. Braidotti thinks of time not as an empty line between events but as continuous becoming: at every moment something is happening, even when it seems nothing is. Life, which she calls zoe, doesn't stop — the body breathes, connections go on, the world around you changes. Waiting doesn't have to be an empty gap between "before" and "after". It is also part of your life, with its own sounds, people and small tasks. You don't have to force yourself not to think about the outcome. You can wait and, at the same time, notice that life is going on right now — and the pause becomes a little less empty.
waiting.practice: While you wait, see one simple task through — water a plant, make tea, sew on a button — and note to yourself: this has already happened.

regret.text: A river never flows backwards, yet carries all that ever flowed into it — Braidotti sees a human life this way. Regret for what you did or didn't do keeps returning you to crossroads long behind you. Braidotti, following Deleuze, understands the human being not as an unchanging essence but as a process of becoming. The person who made that choice is you, and yet not quite you: you have changed since then, in many ways thanks to that very choice. She values "transformation": the pain of the past isn't erased, but it can become material for new connections and new strength. Regret is a sign of what matters to you and of the fact that you keep changing. The past can't be rewritten, but you can influence what it becomes in the rest of your life: a lesson, care for someone, a different choice in a similar situation.
regret.practice: Write one sentence: what has this regret taught me about what I truly value? It is a tributary the river is already carrying.

longing.text: A mycelium links trees in a forest underground, letting them share nourishment even at a distance — Braidotti thinks of human bonds in a similar way. When you miss a particular person, their absence is felt almost physically. Braidotti holds that we are made of connections: another person is not an external object but part of how you live, feel and think. So when they aren't around, it feels as though a piece of you is missing. Such longing is evidence of how real the connection was. And it doesn't vanish entirely — what this person gave you lives on in your habits, words and tastes. Her ethics suggests not freezing in the pain but letting the connection continue in new forms: through memory, gratitude and what you pass on.
longing.practice: Recall one habit or phrase you picked up from this person and use it on purpose today — let the bond work, like mycelium underground.

world_pain.text: "We are all in this together, but we are not one and the same" — Braidotti returns to this formula again and again. Pain for the world — wars, injustice, heavy news — can feel unbearable, and the formula helps explain why. We are connected to other people, to animals and to the whole planet, which is why others' pain echoes in us; it is a sign of living connection, not weakness. But Braidotti also warns that it is impossible to bear everything alone. Her affirmative ethics is not naive optimism but a decision to keep living and acting together with others despite the pain, and to protect your own strength so as not to burn out. You are not obliged to hold all the grief of the world inside you. You can choose one thread — one cause, one person, one community — and hold on to it.
world_pain.practice: Give the news half an hour less today, and spend the freed time on one thread: help a neighbour, support one good local effort, call someone who is struggling.

rejection.text: A snapshot is easy to throw away, a river's current is not — this is roughly how Braidotti sees a person. Rejection wounds deeply: it feels as though not an offer but you as a whole were turned down. Braidotti describes the human being as a nomadic subject — not a finished portrait but a process, a multitude of connections and possibilities. One encounter, one form of connection can be rejected, but not the whole of that movement at once. Moreover, in her view any connection depends on both sides, on their strength, circumstances and timing; the fact that it didn't come together is not a verdict on one person. Rejection means this connection didn't happen right now — it says nothing about your worth. The pain is honest, and it deserves to be lived through. But your capacity to form connections hasn't gone anywhere — it is simply looking for another direction.
rejection.practice: Call or meet someone today with whom it's easy to be yourself — even briefly. Let the river flow where it is welcome.

abandonment.text: A climber holds the rock by three points of contact, not one — Braidotti offers similar wisdom about connections. The fear of being abandoned can be very old, almost childlike — and no less real for that. Braidotti emphasises that we are relational beings, and our vulnerability is tied precisely to this. We are not the autonomous fortresses that classical humanism painted us as; we depend on one another. This is not a flaw but a shared condition of life, and the fear of losing someone only shows how important that person is. But Braidotti also hints at a way out of the vicious circle: the nomadic subject holds on not to one thread but to many. The more varied your connections — with people, activities, places — the less any single possible loss feels like the end of everything. The fear doesn't disappear, but your support grows wider.
abandonment.practice: Name aloud five threads that hold you apart from this person: people, activities, places, animals. Touch one finger of your hand for each — five points of contact.

unrequited.text: Spinoza defines love as joy accompanied by the image of another — and there isn't a word about reciprocity in that definition. Following him, Braidotti sees love not as lack but as a rise in power, and a strong feeling with nowhere to go is no less real for being unanswered. Even without a response, this force is real: it has changed you, made you more sensitive, opened up something new. Love doesn't have to be an exchange to be meaningful. The other side of the connection didn't respond — that hurts, and it needs to be acknowledged. But the capacity to love that you have discovered in yourself remains yours. Braidotti's affirmative ethics suggests neither renouncing this force nor blaming yourself for it, but gradually letting it flow in other directions too — towards people, activities, yourself.
unrequited.practice: Today, send a bit of this force in another direction: cook something good for yourself, help someone, do something you love. The force remains yours.

humiliation.text: A throne can take a singer's stage but not their voice — this is how Braidotti distinguishes potestas, power that places some above others, from potentia, the inner capacity to live and act. Humiliation is the feeling of being thrown down while everyone watched. Humiliation is an act of potestas: someone uses a hierarchy to make you smaller. But in her view, potestas can wound your position without cancelling your potentia. Your capacity to feel, to connect with others, to act stays with you. Braidotti describes affirmative ethics as a slow, shared process of recovering strength. So you don't have to "swallow" humiliation alone. You can tell someone who is on your side about it — that brings back the sense that you are not alone and not "down below".
humiliation.practice: Write one sentence: "This was about their power, not about my worth." Read it aloud to someone on your side — or to yourself.

body_shame.text: Ancient statues are young, muscular and symmetrical — and Braidotti shows that this ideal of the "proper body" was historically constructed: everything else was measured against it as a deviation. If you are unhappy with your body, that unhappiness often speaks in someone else's voice. Contemporary culture has merely swapped the standards. Braidotti's posthuman view sees the body differently: not as a façade to be adjusted to a norm, but as a living process, a knot of forces and connections, part of zoe — the life shared by all living things. Your body is not a project that failed but that with which you feel, move and embrace. You can shift your attention, even briefly, from how it looks to what it does.
body_shame.practice: Do something where your body is an action, not a picture: stretch, walk barefoot, wrap your palms around a warm cup. Name one thing it did for you today.

illness.text: A forest after a fire doesn't return to how it was, yet lives on in a new rhythm — Braidotti values such resilience over the ideal of invulnerability. When your body lets you down, the world shrinks, and fear, anger and tiredness are entirely legitimate. Braidotti insists that we are "embodied" beings: thought and feeling are inseparable from the body with its rhythms and limits. Classical humanism dreamed of the human as the sovereign master of their body; Braidotti considers this dream an illusion. For her, the body is not a machine that has "broken" but a living process with its own logic, and vulnerability is a shared condition of all living beings. Illness doesn't make you "less of a person". It changes your rhythm and your connections, and within this new rhythm, too, you can look for what sustains the strength to live — people, small things, moments of calm.
illness.practice: Today, accept one act of care without refusing or apologising: tea someone brings, a call, help with chores. Or do such a small thing for yourself.

pride.text: An orchestra sounds because everyone plays, yet the soloist has every right to enjoy their part — Braidotti looks at pride in much this way. Pride in what you have done is a good, legitimate feeling, and it's worth allowing yourself. Braidotti, drawing on Spinoza, understands joy as a growth of potentia — our capacity to act. Pride in something seen through to the end is exactly that kind of joy: you have felt what you are capable of. Her affirmative ethics values such moments because they nourish life. At the same time, Braidotti stresses that we never act alone: behind every achievement there are connections — people, conditions, support, even tools. Pride needs neither to be hidden nor inflated. It can be shared: you can rejoice in your own strength and notice those who helped. Pride like this doesn't wall you off from others; it connects you to them.
pride.practice: Tell someone about what you did, and in the same conversation name one person or thing that helped. Be glad about both, out loud.

melancholy.text: For years Braidotti has argued against the "melancholic" tone of critical thought — the habit of seeing in the world nothing but loss, decline and the end. But a gentle, bright sadness, quiet and pensive, that you don't want to chase away is a different feeling. Her quarrel is with the pose of hopelessness, not with the delicate sadness that makes us sensitive. Melancholy can be a form of attention — to fragility, to what is passing, to the fact that everything alive is changeable and in the process of becoming. Such sadness doesn't take away the strength to live; it deepens your connection with the world. Affirmative ethics doesn't demand that you hurry to replace it with joy. It invites you to notice what tenderness towards the world this sadness carries within it, and to let it be part of your movement.
melancholy.practice: Spend a minute watching something passing — a sunset, a cloud, a falling leaf — and let yourself feel sad about it tenderly. Sadness, too, can be a form of attention.
